prompt: Lesson 3's linkbox answered with `Server: gunicorn` and none of the browser's protective headers, and lesson 3's Bandit and Semgrep raised nothing about either. Why?

choices.text: The rules were tuned too loosely in lesson 3
choices.why: Lesson 3 tuned B101 in tests and nothing else; no rule there looks for a header that is absent.

choices.text: Neither is a line in the code they read
choices.why: Right. The banner comes from gunicorn and the headers are an absence; a static tool reads lines that are there.

choices.text: Static analysis cannot read Python web frameworks
choices.why: Bandit found the SQL in Flask code in lesson 3; it reads the framework's code fine.

choices.text: The headers only appear behind a reverse proxy
choices.why: linkbox sends nothing at all, proxy or not; the curl to staging shows it.

prompt: Which defect could the baseline scan of this lesson never find in linkbox, however long it ran?

choices.text: A missing header on the 404 page
choices.why: The spider asks for robots.txt and sitemap.xml, both 404s, and the first scan's 10038 listed one of them.

choices.text: A server banner in every response
choices.why: Banners are read from ordinary responses; that is what passive rules are for.

choices.text: A flaw in the code that handles `POST /links`
choices.why: Right. The route needs the token, the spider never reached it, and a scan judges only what it reaches.

choices.text: A missing `X-Frame-Options` on the search page
choices.why: It found exactly that: 10020 on `/search?q=ZAP`.

prompt: Where in the pipeline can a dynamic scan run, at the earliest?

choices.text: Before the tests, straight on the fresh checkout
choices.why: A checkout is files; there is nothing running to send a request to.

choices.text: After the build, once the image runs
choices.why: Right. It needs a running instance of what was built, so it comes after the build.

choices.text: In the editor, as the code is typed
choices.why: That is where some static checks run; a dynamic one needs a service.

choices.text: In the pre-commit hook
choices.why: A hook sees staged files, not a running service.

prompt: `ci/dast.sh` names its network `linkbox-staging-$$`. What does `$$` buy?

choices.text: A name Docker accepts, since networks need a number
choices.why: Docker accepts `linkbox-staging` as it is; the staging section made exactly that by hand.

choices.text: Two runs at once cannot collide
choices.why: Right. `$$` is the script's process id, different for every run.

choices.text: The scan report can be matched to its commit
choices.why: The commit is in `CI_COMMIT`; a process id says nothing about it.

choices.text: The trap knows which network to keep
choices.why: The trap removes the network; it keeps nothing.

prompt: With the service running on the staging network, `curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/` from the host fails to connect. Why?

choices.text: gunicorn listens only on 127.0.0.1 inside the container
choices.why: The Dockerfile binds 0.0.0.0:8000, and the scanner on the network reached it.

choices.text: The service had not started yet
choices.why: The ZAP container's curl got an answer a moment earlier.

choices.text: Port 8000 is taken on the host
choices.why: A taken port is a different error, on a different command; nothing was bound here.

choices.text: `docker run` published no port
choices.why: Right. The service is reachable on its own network and nowhere else, on purpose.

prompt: A team scans a shared test server that three teams deploy to. A header warning appears on Tuesday and is gone on Wednesday, with no commit to the service in between. What would the per-run staging of this lesson have removed?

choices.text: The scanner's own false positives
choices.why: A false positive is a rule misreading a response; this is the response itself changing.

choices.text: A result that depends on what other people left on the server
choices.why: Right. A staging made from the commit's image and thrown away answers only for that commit.

choices.text: The need for a rules file
choices.why: The rules decide what a finding does; they cannot make the target stable.

choices.text: The time the spider spends crawling
choices.why: The spider crawls the same way on either target.

prompt: The scan is run with `-z -silent`. What does `-silent` stop?

choices.text: ZAP printing the rules that passed
choices.why: That is what `grep -v ^PASS` did here; `-silent` does not change the output.

choices.text: ZAP sending requests that could break the service
choices.why: The baseline never sends those; that is the passive mode, not this flag.

choices.text: ZAP calling out on its own: update checks, add-ons, news
choices.why: Right. A CI job should not need outbound access, tell a third party it is scanning, or change rules between runs.

choices.text: ZAP writing its plan into `/zap/wrk`
choices.why: That failed because the mount is read-only, a different decision in `ci/dast.sh`.

prompt: How many URLs did ZAP's spider find in linkbox?
Match each rule the baseline raised to what it is about.

pairs.right: another site loading the page inside a frame
the browser guessing a response's type from its bytes
the value sent coming back inside an HTML attribute
nothing limiting what the page may load

right_distractors: the session cookie lacking its Secure flag

prompt: The first baseline run, with no rules file, exited with status 2. What does 2 say?

choices.text: At least one WARN, and no FAIL
choices.why: Right. With no rules file every rule is a WARN, so the default says no more than that.

choices.text: Two rules matched
choices.why: Four matched; the status is a category, not a count.

choices.text: The scan could not finish
choices.why: That is 3; this scan finished and printed its totals.

choices.text: At least one rule set to FAIL matched
choices.why: That is 1, and no rule can be FAIL without a rules file.

prompt: In `ci/zap-rules.conf`, the action that stops the build when its rule matches is ___
What is the `trap … EXIT` line in `ci/dast.sh` for?

choices.text: It turns ZAP's exit status into the stage's
choices.why: The status of the last command already is the script's; the trap only cleans up.

choices.text: It stops the scan if it runs past a minute
choices.why: Nothing in the script times the scan; `-m` sets the spider's minutes.

choices.text: It deletes the container and network however the script ends
choices.why: Right. A failed scan would otherwise leave a running service for the next run to trip over.

choices.text: It waits for gunicorn before the scan starts
choices.why: That is the `sleep 2`, a cruder thing.

prompt: Put what `ci/dast.sh` does in the order it happens.
items: create a network named after the script's process
start the image of this commit on it
run the baseline from a second container with the rules
remove the container and the network

prompt: The scan already checks the headers every night. Why does the fix come with a unit test as well?

choices.text: The test runs on every push and names what broke
choices.why: Right. It takes under a second. The scan would find a regression the next night; the test finds it on the push that caused it.

choices.text: ZAP cannot read the headers of a 404 page
choices.why: It read them: in the first scan, 10038 listed `sitemap.xml`, a 404.

choices.text: The scan sees only the image, not the code
choices.why: That is true and it is why the scan is useful; it is not why the test exists.

choices.text: Rules set to FAIL do not break the build at night
choices.why: A FAIL breaks the nightly run as it would any other.

prompt: 10031 is a false positive on today's search page. Why is it left at WARN instead of being set to IGNORE?

choices.text: ZAP refuses IGNORE for any rule about cross-site scripting
choices.why: Any rule can be ignored; the file accepts it.

choices.text: A WARN breaks the nightly build, so it gets read
choices.why: With `-I`, a WARN breaks nothing in this lesson.

choices.text: IGNORE works per rule, so it would hide a future real one
choices.why: Right. The file works per rule, not per page, so ignoring it would hide a real one later.

choices.text: The rule may be right after all
choices.why: The response settles it for this page; the reason is about pages not written yet.

prompt: What in linkbox's response shows that 10031 is a false positive?

choices.text: The search page answers 200, not 500
choices.why: That shows the search works, not whether the value is escaped.

choices.text: The page carries a Content-Security-Policy
choices.why: The policy is a second line of defence; the rule is about the value in the attribute.

choices.text: The word `ZAP` is in the `value` attribute
choices.why: That is what made the rule match, not what clears it.

choices.text: A double quote sent in `q` came back as `"`
choices.why: Right. Escaped, the quote cannot end the attribute, so the text cannot become markup.

prompt: Which of these are true of the `after_request` function added to `app.py`? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: It adds the headers to Flask's 404 pages too
choices.why: Right: the curl for `/nothing-here` came back with all three.

choices.text: A route added later gets the headers with no change
choices.why: Right: the function runs for every response, whatever route made it.

choices.text: It changes how Jinja escapes the search value
choices.why: Escaping is Jinja's and was already on; the function only sets headers.

choices.text: It makes the dynamic scan unnecessary
choices.why: The scan checks the image as started, which a unit test of the code does not.

prompt: Why does `dast` go in `ci/nightly` rather than in `ci/stages`?

choices.text: It is too slow to wait for on every push
choices.why: Right: it needs an image, a container and a crawl, and the unit test covers the headers on every push meanwhile.

choices.text: ZAP may only run once a day under its licence
choices.why: ZAP is open source with no such limit.

choices.text: Its findings are only warnings
choices.why: Three of its rules FAIL; where it runs is about time.

choices.text: Main is the only branch with a built image
choices.why: Every push builds an image, on every branch.

prompt: A colleague proposes a weekly `zap-full-scan.py` against linkbox's production address: "it's our own service, so it's allowed". What is the answer the lesson gives?

choices.text: Fine, as long as it runs at night when traffic is low
choices.why: Night changes who notices, not what the scan writes into real data.

choices.text: Fine, with `-silent` so nobody outside is told
choices.why: `-silent` stops ZAP calling out; it does nothing about what the scan sends in.

choices.text: No: run it against a staging made for the run
choices.why: Right. An active scan writes and breaks things, so it points at a throwaway target, even one you own.

choices.text: No: active scans are never worth running
choices.why: They find what the baseline cannot; the question is where they point.

prompt: The nightly scan passes with one warning. With no authentication configured, what does that pass assert?

choices.text: linkbox has no web vulnerabilities
choices.why: The scan read four URLs and sent nothing to provoke a flaw; it asserts much less.

choices.text: The pages a stranger reaches sent the expected headers
choices.why: Right. Everything behind the token was never scanned.

choices.text: Every route, `POST /links` included, was checked
choices.why: `POST /links` needs the token and was not among the URLs found.

choices.text: The image matches what was reviewed
choices.why: Nothing in this scan compares the image with a review; lesson 14 deals with identity.

prompt: A partner company gives you the address of its API, and a teammate wants to run the baseline against it to check its headers before integrating. What comes first?

choices.text: Nothing: the baseline only reads, so it needs no permission
choices.why: It still sends the spider's requests to a system you do not own; reading is not the same as being allowed.

choices.text: Running it with `-silent` so the partner is not told
choices.why: Hiding a scan from the owner is the opposite of what is needed.

choices.text: Written permission from the partner to scan it
choices.why: Right. Their system, their decision, on the record; or ask them for their own results.

choices.text: A rules file that sets every rule to WARN
choices.why: Rules decide what a finding does to your build, not whether you may scan.

prompt: A later commit deletes the `@app.after_request` line by accident. Where is it caught first?

choices.text: In the nightly scan, as three FAILs
choices.why: The scan would catch it too, but only that night.

choices.text: In Semgrep, in the sast stage
choices.why: No rule of lesson 3 knows about headers.

choices.text: In the test stage of that push
choices.why: Right. `test_every_answer_carries_the_headers` fails in the push that removed them.

choices.text: At review, since the diff is one line
choices.why: A one-line diff is the easiest to miss; the test does not depend on anybody noticing.
